title: How easy is it to steal a nuclear bomb?
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant discuss how easy it would be to steal a nuclear weapon. They open with Back to the Future and The Manhattan Project references, then cover the post-Soviet dispersal of roughly 27,000 tactical and strategic nukes and their return to Russia, the likelihood of stealing components versus whole bombs, A.Q. Khan's nuclear proliferation network, explosive and fissile material requirements, fission versus fusion bombs, unaccounted-for plutonium and highly enriched uranium, strategic versus tactical nukes, security measures like permissive action links and the Wargames two-man rule, the dirty bomb threat, the 2002 Siberian uranium shipment incident, depleted uranium, the Los Alamos security breach, the Broken Arrow designation, Cold War nuclear accidents (including the 1950 Mars Bluff crater, the 1960 Sea of Japan aircraft loss, and a near-drop during a submarine transfer), IAEA figures on lost radioactive material, and the state of international nuclear treaties. The episode ends with a listener mail about a happiness survey at Collegiate Academy in Erie, Pennsylvania, inspired by Bhutan's Gross National Happiness.

segments.title: Opening sponsor reads and intro
segments.summary: Sponsor reads for the Reinvented 2012 Camry and Altoids tins open the episode, followed by the hosts' introduction.

segments.title: Opening banter: Back to the Future and The Manhattan Project
segments.summary: Hosts joke about Back to the Future, the Biff actor, and its plutonium subplot, then mention The Manhattan Project film about a teen stealing enriched uranium.

segments.title: Post-Soviet nuclear arsenal and transport risk
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the roughly 27,000 Soviet tactical and strategic nukes after the USSR dissolved, and how they were moved back into Russia, with transport as a vulnerable point.

segments.title: Stealing components versus whole bombs; A.Q. Khan
segments.summary: They argue stealing components and assembling a bomb may be more likely than stealing a whole warhead, and describe A.Q. Khan's role in selling nuclear knowledge, including his house arrest.

segments.title: Fission versus fusion bombs and required materials
segments.summary: The hosts explain fission and fusion, the role of TNT in triggering a fission chain reaction, and why highly enriched uranium or plutonium is the hardest material to obtain.

segments.title: Unaccounted nuclear material and strategic vs tactical nukes
segments.summary: They discuss Robert Gates' 2008 claim that Moscow could not account for all its plutonium and enriched uranium, and distinguish strategic nukes (deterrence) from tactical nukes (battlefield use).

segments.title: Security measures, Permissive Action Links and WarGames
segments.summary: Standard security measures are covered, along with concern about insider employment, and the permissive action link two-person rule shown in WarGames.

segments.title: Dirty bombs, 2002 Siberian uranium shipment, and depleted uranium
segments.summary: The hosts describe dirty bombs made from nuclear junk, a 2002 Siberian border seizure of uranium later described as depleted, and concerns about depleted uranium ammunition.

segments.title: Los Alamos breach, Broken Arrow and lost bombs
segments.summary: They cover the 2006 Los Alamos security breach involving access control information, the Navy's Broken Arrow term, and the lost Tybee Island nuke.

segments.title: Cold War nuclear accidents
segments.summary: The hosts recount the Mars Bluff crater accident, the 1960 aircraft loss into the Sea of Japan, and a near-drop during a submarine-to-ship transfer, along with the Defense Department's claim of at least one serious accident per year.

segments.title: IAEA lost material statistics and nonproliferation treaties
segments.summary: They cite IAEA figures on lost or stolen radioactive sources in 2006 and note the gap in international treaties, and argue nonproliferation must be rethought after the Cold War.
topics: Physical Protection of Nuclear Material Convention

segments.title: Listener mail: Collegiate Academy happiness survey
segments.summary: A listener from Erie, Pennsylvania describes a student project measuring happiness at her school, modeled on Bhutan's Gross National Happiness, with the school scoring 3.58 out of 5.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts invite listener email and close with sponsor reads.
